$comment: THE NUMBER THAT CAN GO RED AFTER THE RELEASE.
Everything this repository does about a bad change happens BEFORE the push: seventeen
gates, a rubric review, a perf budget on the e2e lane, and `.husky/pre-push` running the
whole chain because Vercel ships `master` on push and a required status check never sees
that landing path. Past the push there was one signal and it was binary:
`scripts/post-deploy-verify.mjs` asked `/api/health` whether the deployment ANSWERS.
A deployment that answers can still be broken. `/api/health` returns `ok: true` for a
release that made every page four times slower, and for one whose homepage now 500s —
the probe never asks. So the first report of a degraded release was somebody opening the
app, and `npm run revert:drill` — a rehearsed, timed rollback — was waiting on a human
noticing a symptom. A rehearsal with no trigger is a rehearsal.
This file is the trigger's input: a small set of routes on the DEPLOYED host, each with
the response time it may not pass and the reason it earns one, plus a ceiling on how many
samples may fail outright. `scripts/post-deploy-verify.mjs` measures them after the health
probe comes back clean, and a breach FAILS the post-deploy run — with the promote-previous
rollback command printed next to it, the same one the drill rehearses.
WHAT IT DOES NOT DO, and this is deliberate rather than unfinished: it does not revert.
An automatic revert means a token that can write `refs/heads/master` on a repository where
that push IS a release under the operator's name, which AGENTS.md § Red says never. The
verify job holds `contents: read`. What this produces is the dated, automatic ANSWER the
rehearsed rollback was always waiting for; arming the revert leg is a decision an operator
makes with a token.
WHAT IS MEASURED. The DOCUMENT RESPONSE — the wall clock from issuing the request to the
server committing the response, read without following redirects and without downloading
sub-resources. It is the half of a page's cost this repository's code owns, and it is the
same choice `.github/perf-budgets.json` makes for the e2e lane, so a reader meets one
definition rather than two. Warm (`warmups` requests thrown away, because a serverless
function's first invocation after a deploy is a cold start and a fact about the platform)
and best-of-`samples`, because a shared runner stalls and a route that is genuinely twice
as slow is slow in every sample.
THE ROUTE LIST IS SHORT ON PURPOSE. This is the one budget in the repository that can fail
a RELEASE, so a route listed here that 404s on the deployment is a red build about the
list rather than about the release. Every entry is a public, key-free page that exists in
`src/app` and answers anonymously; `test-unit/post-deploy-budget.test.mjs` holds each one
to a real page module on every build. Adding one is cheap and adding a wrong one is not.
THE NUMBERS ARE CEILINGS, NOT TARGETS, and they are UNMEASURED — `baseline` is null,
because nothing has yet run this against the production host and recorded what these
routes actually cost. They are generous on purpose (ADR-0007: a check blocks where it
passes). Every run writes its measurements into `post-deploy.json`, which the workflow
keeps for 90 days, so the first green release produces exactly the numbers a tighter
ceiling needs. TIGHTEN THEM WITH THE REASON IN THE SAME DIFF; never raise one to make your
own release pass — that is rubric B3, and a budget nobody can fail is the cheapest green
in this repository.

metric.why: The server's answer for the route, warm, best of three — the same definition .github/perf-budgets.json uses, so the pre-merge budget and the post-deploy one are measuring the same thing on two hosts.

errorRate.why: A route in this list that answers a non-2xx, or does not answer at all, is not slow — it is down, and it is down on a release that already shipped. Zero is the only defensible ceiling for a list this short and this public; a non-zero one would mean deciding in advance which of four public pages may be broken.

notCovered: Authenticated pages. Everything under /app needs a session, and a post-deploy probe holding one would need a real account's cookie in CI — a credential this repository will not move (AGENTS.md § Red). The public shell at /dashboard renders the same composition for the anonymous sample tenant and is the proxy.

Error RATE in the statistical sense. This samples four routes a handful of times a minute after the deploy; it catches a release that is broken, not one that fails 2% of requests. That number lives in a platform's own telemetry and .github/environments.json § cannotSee already says which half of production this repository cannot see.
Anything after the first few minutes. The probe runs on the release event and then stops. A regression that only appears under Monday-morning load is not this check's job and is not claimed to be.
The AI routes. They spend money per call and the budget would be measuring a provider. /api/health already reports whether they are configured.

routes.label: Homepage
routes.why: The marketing entry point and the most-linked page in the product — the one URL where a slow or broken release is visible to everyone immediately. Rendered from fixtures with no store and no model, so time spent here is time spent in the render path.

routes.label: Pricing
routes.why: The page a release must never break, because it is the one that carries the plans and the prices. It is nearly static, so a ceiling this generous can only be passed by something structural.

routes.label: Demo app shell
routes.why: The heaviest public composition — the whole authed shell rendered for the anonymous sample tenant, and the closest key-free proxy for what a signed-in page costs. A store change that stops deduping its reads lands here first.

routes.label: Campaign triage
routes.why: The heaviest public READ: the campaign store plus the triage ranking. It shares its render path with the authed product's busiest module, which is why it is worth a number on the deployed host and not only on the e2e lane's dev server.

probe.why: The readiness probe itself, which does a real one-document Firestore read behind the CRON_SECRET guard. It is the only measured route that touches the store, so it is the number that moves when the store — rather than the render path — is the thing that got slower. Generous, because a cold serverless invocation plus a round trip to Firestore is not a fast operation and this must not teach anyone to re-run a release.
